learningObjective: Explain the Halide/TVM compute-vs-schedule separation and identify what tiling changes in the resulting loop nest.

canonicalClaims.claim: In Halide/TVM, compute (the semantic description of the output) is separated from schedule (loop-level primitives such as split, reorder, tile, fuse, vectorize). Schedule transformations restructure the loop nest without changing what is computed, so long as they respect dependence constraints.
conditions: The schedule primitives obey dependence rules (e.g., not reordering a reduction dim that lacks associativity guarantees).
nonImplications: Does not imply the same compute can be scheduled optimally on every hardware target.
Does not imply that reordering a reduction dim is safe under FP (associativity is not exact for finite-precision floats).

sourceMappings.locator: TVM schedule primitives; compute vs. schedule

misconceptions.claim: Tiling changes the arithmetic done at each output; you must re-verify numerical correctness.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Tiling reorders iteration only; the arithmetic per element is unchanged when the reduction order is preserved.

misconceptions.claim: Tiling is the mechanism used to fuse adjacent operators in the graph IR.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Tiling is a loop-level schedule primitive; operator fusion is a graph-/operator-IR concern.

misconceptions.claim: Schedules that split loops are equivalent to strength reduction.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Strength reduction replaces expensive ops with cheaper equivalents; tiling reorganizes iteration.

misconceptions.claim: Applying a schedule always improves performance.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Poorly chosen tile sizes can hurt locality, reduce parallelism, or increase register pressure; good schedules are search-driven or expert-tuned.

implementationFacts: Halide/TVM schedule primitives: split, reorder, fuse, tile, vectorize, parallelize, unroll
The compute is invariant under schedule; the schedule only affects codegen
Reduction reorder requires FP-associativity considerations (or exact-integer types)
performanceScenarios: Tiling improves cache locality by reusing tile-resident data across the inner iteration space, especially for GEMM and stencil kernels.
